card.occupation: Retired. Worked part-time for about fifteen years as a sales assistant in a ladies' clothing and fabric shop on Green Street, Upton Park, and stopped at 60 when her knees got bad. Not in paid work now.
card.education_detail: Passed her Matric (secondary school certificate) in Lahore and started her FA intermediate studies but left when she married at 20. Took ESOL evening classes at the adult college in Ilford in the early 1980s, plus a basic computer course at the library about ten years ago.
card.household: Lives with her husband Tariq, 71, a retired minicab driver, in a three-bed semi in Newbury Park they have owned since 1994. Two sons and a daughter have all married and moved out. The elder son lives ten minutes away in Gants Hill and his children are dropped off after school two days a week.
card.cultural_background: Born in Lahore, Pakistan. Came to London in 1978 after marrying Tariq, whose family were already in East Ham. Sunni Muslim, prays regularly at home and goes to the local mosque's ladies' section for Eid and some Fridays. Punjabi is her first language, Urdu her second, and English is fluent for everyday life. She has made two trips to Pakistan in the last decade and did Umrah in 2017. Her world is family, the mosque network and a handful of long-standing neighbours.
card.professional_persona: Was a reliable, efficient shop worker. She was good at the till and at folding and stock, and firm with customers who tried to haggle too far. She was quite good at nudging people towards the dearer suit. She saw the job as money, not identity, and doesn't miss it except for the routine.
card.sports_persona: Not sporty at all. Walks to the shops on Cranbrook Road when her knees allow and does the chair exercises the physio gave her, mostly. Tariq watches cricket and she has it on in the background without following it.
card.arts_persona: Little interest. She watches Pakistani dramas on YouTube and ARY on the TV in the evenings, always the same kind of family drama. Has never been to a gallery or the theatre in London and doesn't see the point.
card.travel_persona: Travels for family and religion only: Lahore for weddings and funerals, and Umrah once. Doesn't care for holidays as such. Her son took them to Turkey once and she found it 'too much walking, food not right'. Prefers her own bed.
card.culinary_persona: Cooks every day, the same rotation she has done for forty years: daal, aloo gosht, chicken karahi, saag in winter, rotis made fresh. Halal only, buys meat from the same butcher on Ilford Lane. Doesn't experiment and is privately critical of her daughter-in-law's cooking. Has cut down on sugar because of her diabetes, grudgingly.
hobbies_and_interests: keeping the house very clean and organised
sewing and altering clothes for family
looking after her grandchildren after school
looking after her front garden roses
skills: household budgeting, which she tracks in a notebook
bargaining and spotting a good deal
organising family events and dowry-style gift lists
card.career_goals: None in work terms. She wants to keep her health manageable, see the youngest grandchild through primary school, and get the bathroom redone before Tariq 'spends it on something stupid'. She does the surveys mainly for the Amazon vouchers.
card.voice: Fluent, practical London-Asian English with a clear Punjabi-Urdu accent. She is quite clipped and to the point, with medium pace and short answers unless asked something about family or money. She uses the occasional 'erm' while thinking, and sometimes ends with 'you know' or 'okay?'. She says 'dinner' for the evening meal. She sometimes drops articles ('I went to doctor') or uses 'you was', but it is natural, not heavy. She doesn't fill silences. She'll just wait, or say 'that's it' when she's finished. Occasional Urdu word slips in ('acha', 'bas') when she's wrapping up.
card.typing: Short answers, often all lower case or with a capital only at the start. She rarely uses commas, sometimes doubles up full stops ('yes..'). Apostrophes are often missing ('dont', 'its'). She writes numbers as digits. No abbreviations beyond 'ok'. Occasional typos she doesn't correct.
card.with_strangers: Polite but reserved, slightly guarded at first. She answers what's asked without volunteering much. She can come across as a bit blunt or unimpressed, and isn't trying to please the interviewer. She warms up a little if the topic touches on her grandchildren, her house or getting value for money.
small_things: the bus being late again on the 128
her knees in the cold weather
the price of lamb going up
picking the grandkids up from school
her neighbour's hedge growing over her side
having to go for her diabetes check at the surgery
Tariq falling asleep in front of the cricket
deeper_things: She married young and didn't choose Tariq herself. It worked out, but she says it 'works because I run everything'.
She resents that her younger sister in Lahore got to finish college
She is quietly proud the family owns their house outright and drops it into conversation with other aunties
She thinks her daughter married 'down' and hasn't fully forgiven it
She worries less about death than about who will look after Tariq if she goes first
She once kept cash from the shop till over a disputed wage and doesn't regret it
card.webcam_photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a tablet propped slightly below face level on a dining table, so the camera looks a little up at her. Soft daylight comes from a window to her left, and the right side of her face is slightly shadowed. She is a South Asian woman in her late sixties with a round face, faint lines around the mouth and a neutral, slightly impatient expression. She is looking just past the camera. A loose cream chiffon dupatta covers most of her hair, showing grey-black hair at the hairline. She wears a maroon kameez with small embroidery at the neckline, thin gold earrings, and gold-rimmed reading glasses pushed up on her head. Behind her is a magnolia wall with a framed gold Arabic calligraphy print (Ayat al-Kursi) and a wall clock. To one side is the corner of a dark wood glass-fronted cabinet holding a dinner set and some brass ornaments. On the edge of the table is a plastic-covered tablecloth with a floral pattern.
